The work showed that the two materials were incompatible to a certain extent due to phase separation during processing. Furthermore, the LC materials will often “activate” (become electroactive) at different temperatures than the terpolymer matrix. While our results indicated that incorporation of LCs did not have a profound impact on electrocaloric performance, they also did not reduce performance. We believe that further exploration is needed for LC containing EC films. The results of this work show that electrospray processing can create thin electrocaloric films, with necessary breakdown strengths using one of the best EC polymers available today. We found that electrospray processing may also enhance the EC effect, possibly due to the increased order, or crystallinity, observed with electrosprayed films when compared to films made through traditional casting. There are opportunities to translate this technology to commercial practice with additional support and process integration work. 1. Introduction Conventional cooling technology used in heating, venting, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems is based on a vapor compression cycle that has been estimated to consume more than more than 20% of the electricity generated in the world and contribute significantly to greenhouse gases emissions.1 Overall, air conditioning and electric fans accounts for about a fifth of the total electricity consumption today, and energy consumption for cooling purposes in the world is expected to triple by 2050.2 Vapor compression in the refrigeration industry only reaches 60% of operating efficiency, and the efficiency tends to be 20-30% lower when the size of the system reduced.1 The refrigeration market is also continuing to expand, with the compound annual growth rate in the U.S. expected to increase by about 4.3% from 2023 to 20303, and this has the potential to exponentially increase climate change.4 Solid-state cooling technology based on an electrocaloric cycle is a possible alternative to vapor compression systems that may permit the development of more efficient heat pumps with lower global warming potential and more environmentally-friendly materials compared to the conventional vapor compression cooler. The basic theory behind electrocaloric devices is the conversion between thermal energy and electrical energy in an electrocaloric cycle. The entropy of the system leads to the change in thermal energy, and the energy can be modified by both the operating temperature and the applied field.5,6 The cooling occurs through adiabatic depolarization whereas the heating occurs through adiabatic polarization under a constant electric field.5 Figure 1 (adapted from reference6) demonstrates the process of the EC cycle in detail. 5 DE-EE0009099 The goal of this proposal is to create the next generation electrocaloric materials having nearly a 2-5 X improvement in temperature lift, dielectric breakdown strength, and activation in an electric field. Such an advance will fundamentally transform the residential, commercial and aerospace HVAC industry by enabling highly efficient true solid state based cooling systems.
